examples.solution_text:
Rows represent the first die and columns represent the second. Each cell records an ordered pair.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} &1&2&3&4\\\hline 1&(1,1)&(1,2)&(1,3)&(1,4)\\2&(2,1)&(2,2)&(2,3)&(2,4)\\3&(3,1)&(3,2)&(3,3)&(3,4)\\4&(4,1)&(4,2)&(4,3)&(4,4)\end{array}$
There are $4\times4=16$ equally likely cells.

(a) The favourable pairs are $(2,4),(3,3),(3,4),(4,2),(4,3),(4,4)$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{sum at least }6)&=\frac{6}{16}\\&=\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$

(b) The favourable pairs are $(1,3),(2,4),(3,1),(4,2)$. Both orders count.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{difference }2)&=\frac{4}{16}\\&=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$

(c) The rows contain $0,1,2,3$ favourable cells respectively.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{first greater})&=\frac{0+1+2+3}{16}\\&=\frac{3}{8}\end{aligned}$

Let $R$ mean red and $B$ mean blue. At every stage, the red branch has probability $\frac35$ and the blue branch has probability $\frac25$.
The complete paths are:
$\begin{array}{cccc}RRR&RRB&RBR&RBB\\BRR&BRB&BBR&BBB\end{array}$
There are $2\times2\times2=8$ colour paths, but they are not equally likely. Multiply the branch probabilities for each relevant path.

(a)
$\begin{aligned}P(RRR)&=\frac35\times\frac35\times\frac35\\&=\frac{27}{125}\end{aligned}$

(b) Exactly two reds occur on $RRB,RBR,BRR$.
$\begin{aligned}P(RRB)&=\frac35\times\frac35\times\frac25=\frac{18}{125}\\P(RBR)&=\frac35\times\frac25\times\frac35=\frac{18}{125}\\P(BRR)&=\frac25\times\frac35\times\frac35=\frac{18}{125}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{exactly two reds})&=P(RRB)+P(RBR)+P(BRR)\\&=\frac{18}{125}+\frac{18}{125}+\frac{18}{125}\\&=\frac{54}{125}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A fair five-section spinner numbered $1$ to $5$ is spun four times independently. Find the probability of obtaining at least one $5$.
examples.solution_text:
The complement of at least one $5$ is no $5$s. On each spin, four of the five sections are not $5$.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{no }5\text{s})&=\frac45\times\frac45\times\frac45\times\frac45\\&=\frac{256}{625}\end{aligned}$
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{at least one }5)&=1-P(\text{no }5\text{s})\\&=1-\frac{256}{625}\\&=\frac{369}{625}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: A box contains $5$ caramel chocolates and $6$ mint chocolates. Three chocolates are selected at random without replacement. Find the probability of selecting exactly one caramel chocolate.
examples.solution_text:
Let $C$ mean caramel and $M$ mean mint. Exactly one caramel occurs on the paths $CMM,MCM,MMC$.
The total number remaining decreases from $11$ to $10$ to $9$. Update the remaining flavour counts along each path.
$\begin{aligned}P(CMM)&=\frac5{11}\times\frac6{10}\times\frac59=\frac{150}{990}\\P(MCM)&=\frac6{11}\times\frac5{10}\times\frac59=\frac{150}{990}\\P(MMC)&=\frac6{11}\times\frac5{10}\times\frac59=\frac{150}{990}\end{aligned}$
Add the three favourable path probabilities.
$\begin{aligned}P(\text{exactly one caramel})&=P(CMM)+P(MCM)+P(MMC)\\&=\frac{150}{990}+\frac{150}{990}+\frac{150}{990}\\&=\frac5{11}\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: The ordered-pair array contains 16 equally likely cells. Six have sum at least 6, four have absolute difference 2, and six have first score greater than second. The probabilities are 3/8, 1/4 and 3/8.
Fail probabilities are 0.4 and 0.25. Independent paths give PP = 0.6×0.75 = 0.45, FP = 0.4×0.75 = 0.30, and exactly one pass = 0.6×0.25 + 0.4×0.75 = 0.45. Tree labels agree.

Three reds has probability (3/5)^3 = 27/125. Each of RRB, RBR and BRR has probability 18/125, giving 54/125. The array lists all eight distinct colour paths and correctly distinguishes them from equally likely outcomes.
No 5 in four independent spins has probability (4/5)^4 = 256/625. Its complement is 1−256/625 = 369/625.

Without replacement, RR, RB, BR and BB have probabilities 12/72, 20/72, 20/72 and 20/72, summing to 1. Thus two reds = 1/6, one of each = 5/9, same colour = 4/9, and at least one red = 13/18. All tree branches match the remaining counts.
